items.headline: AI-designed gene-editing enzymes expand the CRISPR toolbox
items.excerpt: Scientists used the ESM Inverse Folding (ESM-IF1) AI protein-design model to generate synthetic TnpB gene-editing enzymes, dubbed SynTnpBs, starting from the known TnpB structure. In a study published in Science, several AI-designed variants outperformed the natural reference enzyme, reaching roughly 46-50% editing efficiency in human cells versus 28% for the original, expanding the compact genome-editing toolbox beyond CRISPR-Cas.

items.headline: AI tool predicts how DNA sequences switch on genes across different cell types
items.excerpt: Martin Vingron's bioinformatics group at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics built Corgi (Context-aware Regulatory Genomics Inference), an AI tool that predicts how the genome behaves — which genes switch on and off — across different cell types. The work could sharpen efforts to model cell activity virtually, with applications in basic research and medicine.

items.headline: New machine-learning tool improves accuracy of genomics research
items.excerpt: University of Virginia researchers identified a widespread, previously unrecognized error in the popular CUT&Tag method used to map the epigenome, and built PATTY, a machine-learning tool that corrects it. The free software improves the reliability of genomics data drawn from very small samples, where chemical and structural modifications of chromosomes control which genes are turned on or off.

items.headline: The emerging field of cognitive brain-computer interfaces
items.excerpt: A review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (Mount Sinai) outlines a roadmap for the next generation of brain-computer interfaces aimed at cognitive disorders — depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD — rather than motor function. Unlike today's movement- and speech-decoding BCIs, cognitive BCIs would rely on AI algorithms that decode dysfunctional brain states in real time and drive adaptive, closed-loop neurostimulation.

items.headline: Scientists built a camera that can track invisible particles in 3D
items.excerpt: An ETH Zurich / EPFL team built PLATON, a particle detector that pairs a light-field (plenoptic) camera and single-photon avalanche-diode sensors with a Transformer-based neural network adapted from large language models to reconstruct particle paths in fast, detailed 3D from a single block of scintillator. Simulations suggest it could match or surpass today's best detectors while replacing millions of components, with potential spillover to sharper PET medical scans.
